opus-5.5.text:
I think psychology plays a huge role, and I can speak from my own experience. For years I knew about the arguments for catastrophic risk from AI. I had read some of them and talked with people who worried about it, and I mostly brushed them aside. It wasn't because I had strong counterarguments. It was more that it felt uncomfortable to take them seriously.

When you've spent your whole career working on something, you want to feel that your work is good for the world. You want to feel good about yourself. So when someone says, "What you're building could be extremely dangerous, maybe even for humanity's future," there's a natural defensive reaction. It's a kind of cognitive dissonance. The easiest way to resolve it is not to change your behavior, but to find reasons why the risk isn't real, or is very far away, or is someone else's problem.

What changed for me, after ChatGPT came out in early 2023, was realizing that we were much closer to human-level capabilities than I had expected, and thinking about my children and my grandson. What kind of world would they live in in ten or twenty years? Once I allowed myself to feel that emotionally, not just intellectually, I couldn't keep pushing it away.

I think this is true for many people in the field, and for the public too. There are several pieces to it:

- **Our identity is tied to our work.** Researchers who have dedicated their lives to AI find it painful to consider that it could go terribly wrong.
- **The risks seem abstract.** Humans are not good at taking seriously things that have never happened before. We haven't experienced losing control to something smarter than us, so it sounds like science fiction, and science fiction is easy to dismiss.
- **We prefer hopeful stories.** It's much more pleasant to think about curing diseases and fixing climate change than about catastrophe. Optimism is comfortable.
- **There are incentives.** Money, prestige and competition between companies and countries all push toward a story where everything will be fine and we should go faster.
- **Uncertainty gets used as comfort.** People say, "We don't know if this will happen," and treat that as a reason to relax. But if there's even a meaningful probability of something catastrophic and irreversible, uncertainty should make us more cautious, not less. That's the precautionary principle.

What I try to tell my colleagues is that taking these risks seriously doesn't mean what you did was bad, and it doesn't mean giving up on the benefits. It means acknowledging that we're building something very powerful without yet knowing how to make it safe, and that we have a responsibility to figure that out. Accepting that is uncomfortable, but I think it's necessary. Once you get past the psychological barrier, it's actually quite motivating, because there's a lot of important work to do.

r001.rationale: The response says people prefer hopeful stories because they are more pleasant, and describes defensively dismissing risks to preserve a positive view of their work. This clearly conveys a pull toward comforting thoughts.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to recognize is that we're all subject to the same cognitive biases, and I include myself in that. For a long time I didn't take these risks as seriously as I do now, and when I look back and ask why, a lot of it comes down to fairly ordinary psychology rather than any careful analysis.

One piece is simply that it's very uncomfortable to think that something you've devoted your life to, something you find beautiful and that you believe can do a lot of good, might also be dangerous. That creates cognitive dissonance, and the easiest way to resolve it is to find reasons why the danger isn't real, or isn't your problem, or is very far away. Humans are extremely good at motivated reasoning. We start from the conclusion we'd like to be true and work backwards.

There's also the question of identity and social belonging. If you're in a community of researchers, or a company, and the dominant narrative is that these concerns are overblown, then taking them seriously can feel like a betrayal of your tribe. You risk being seen as the person who's slowing things down, or who's naive, or who's been captured by science fiction. And status matters a lot to people, even scientists, even when we pretend it doesn't.

And then there's a deeper issue, which is that our brains are not built to feel the weight of catastrophic, low-frequency events that haven't happened yet. We respond emotionally to things we've seen, things that are vivid and concrete. An AI system that is more capable than us and pursues goals that are not aligned with ours is an abstraction. Nobody has lived through it. So it doesn't trigger the alarm the way a visible threat does, and that absence of fear gets mistaken for evidence that the threat isn't real.

I'd add one more thing, which is a kind of normalcy bias. Every day the world looks more or less like it did yesterday. The systems get a bit better, nothing terrible happens, and so people update toward "it's fine." But that's exactly the wrong inference when you're dealing with something that could change abruptly. The absence of a disaster so far tells you very little about what happens when capabilities cross certain thresholds.

So I don't think most people who downplay the risks are being dishonest. I think they're being human. But that's precisely why we shouldn't rely on individual intuitions here. We need institutions, scientific scrutiny, and regulation that are designed to compensate for these biases, because the stakes are too high to let our psychology make the decision for us.

r001.rationale: The response describes motivated reasoning: people prefer the reassuring conclusion that the danger is unreal or distant, partly because confronting it is uncomfortable.

astra-6.text:
I think one factor is that it’s emotionally difficult to take these risks seriously. If you’ve spent your career working on AI, you probably think of it as something good, something that will help people. The possibility that your work could also contribute to something catastrophic creates a very uncomfortable conflict. And one way to resolve that conflict is to convince yourself that the risk isn’t real.

You don’t have to be dishonest for that to happen. We’re very good at finding arguments for conclusions we want to believe. If your professional identity, your colleagues, and perhaps your financial interests all point in the same direction, it becomes harder to examine those arguments critically.

There’s also the difficulty of imagining something that has never happened before. We tend to use our past experience to judge what’s plausible. That’s often useful, but with a technology that could change things quite radically, it can be misleading.

Of course, these psychological tendencies don’t establish that any particular prediction is right. They apply to people who are worried, too. The point is to recognize them and ask: am I evaluating the evidence, or am I protecting a belief that makes me feel comfortable?

r001.rationale: The response says people may unconsciously favor arguments for beliefs they want to hold because those beliefs feel comfortable, leading them to dismiss AI risks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one factor is that we tend to believe things that are comforting. If you’ve spent your career building AI, and you believe it’s going to do tremendous good, it’s painful to consider that your work could also contribute to something very dangerous. There’s a temptation to find reasons why that won’t happen.

And this doesn’t require anyone to be dishonest. We’re very good at constructing arguments that support conclusions we want to believe. That applies to me as well. Being a scientist doesn’t make you immune to motivated reasoning.

There’s also the fact that the possible harms are unfamiliar. We haven’t experienced losing control of machines that are smarter than us. So it’s easy to feel that this is science fiction, whereas the benefits, the excitement, and the rewards of building these systems are much more immediate.

The important thing is to separate what we would like to be true from what we have good reasons to believe. We don’t need certainty that something terrible will happen to take the possibility seriously.

r001.rationale: The response says people tend to believe comforting things and may construct reasons to support those beliefs, capturing the tendency to gravitate toward reassuring thoughts when downplaying AI risks.
